title: Breaking and Entering: Perfume Genius On Using Remixes As Therapy
summary: Mike Hadreas’s ever-morphing pop project Perfume Genius released his fifth album Set My Heart On Fire Immediately last year. Like each album before it, Set My Heart builds and expands on the Perfume Genius sound, upping both the drama and the musical complexity. In keeping with his ever-evolving sound, Mike has just released his first remix album, IMMEDIATELY Remixes, and he calls into Breaking And Entering to explain the origin of the project.
transcript:
Mike Hadreas, who records as Perfume Genius, spoke with Simon Winkler for the 11 March 2021 broadcast, ahead of the release of IMMEDIATELY Remixes, a companion to his fifth album, Set My Heart on Fire Immediately, released by Matador Records in 2020. His music has grown from restrained ballads to elaborate baroque pop; here he discusses creative vulnerability and the comfort of returning to Green Day’s Dookie and Alanis Morissette during quarantine. Edited for length and clarity.

Mike: It wasn’t even conscious. I just realised I was listening to a lot of music I listened to in middle school, not even stuff I particularly liked, but that made me feel like I was back there. Then I was intentionally listening to music. I was making playlists called Hug, just really going for comfort, the playlist.

Simon: What have been the songs you’ve been prescribing for yourself recently?

Mike: I’m very songy. It’s usually a song a week; it could be months. It’s just the one song over and over. One of those songs recently is ‘The Roving’ by Bonny Light Horseman. That’s a recent one too. That’s a rarity for me, for it to be made recently.

The Robert Wyatt song ‘Shipbuilding’ was really heavy for me in the beginning of quarantine. Alice Boman, the whole Alice Boman record that I think she released in the middle of the pandemic, or at the very beginning of it, had that perfect feeling. It was sad and emotional, but it was still really warm and safe feeling. It kind of gave me a place to feel a little bit, but with edges, soft ones.

Simon: Speaking of looking back on culture, there’s a new Twitter account called Tony Soprano Cries to Songs, where the same scene of Tony Soprano driving is matched with different songs. You retweeted the one today featuring ‘Describe’. The account creators were very excited about it.

Mike: That one was kind of for the children, honestly, because they love Tony Soprano. They’re always going off about The Sopranos and Tony Soprano. Maybe all the children are just rediscovering it and going through it in quarantine, binging it. But I watched it when it was out. I haven’t revisited it, but they have this really deep connection with him. I was exploiting that by retweeting it.

Simon: So you had a relationship with the show growing up as well?

Mike: It reminds me of my dad. My dad was deep into it. I’m not rewatching anything that I want to admit to right now, but I have started rewatching things. I keep not wanting to revisit things because I think, I’m going to know everything that happens. It’s not going to be interesting to me. But I literally do not remember anything that happened in these shows.

On The CW, all the teen shows that I watched that I love, there are 23 episodes a season. That’s hundreds of episodes. It can feel cathartic, and sometimes you want something really escapey that almost numbs you out, to zone out. I think I want something kind of campy right now. I need that zany, campy, bad and good combination.

Simon: Listening to a song over and over presents a known emotional experience. With television and films, sometimes you watch something once, but why not keep going back?

Mike: I haven’t really thought about it like that. The songs do become like little anchors. It’s not even explainable. I can tell right away when something washes over you: this is articulating something for me, or helping me process. It’s wiring or rewiring me in the way I need to be, which I haven’t been able to figure out in my daily life.

Simon: You’ve spoken about Set My Heart on Fire Immediately as a way to reflect on your need for connection and draw it into your life. Is the remix album an opportunity to create deeper, wider connections with the artists you’ve approached?

Mike: I think so. It’s almost just the opening, the starting point for it, because it still feels very virtual, very disconnected in a lot of ways, just because we are. Whatever communication we had going into making the remix together, some of it was just, I was a fan. Do you want to do this? And then they did it.

I don’t treat any little piece of my music as sacred. I had no rules for how it was supposed to be treated. I liked them, and whatever they wanted to do, I was going to be happy with. Getting these remixes back, it’s something really powerful and meaningful to me that was made now, made in this time. I haven’t been touring the music I just put out and I haven’t been making anything new. I felt very paralysed, not very creative, not very in touch with that part of me or anybody else.

I’ve made friends through it or got to hear from friends that I usually would see because we were on the road and would meet up, or at a festival. Jenny Hval, we toured together and became friends. I’ve been a really big fan of hers for a long time. I think she had worked on some remixes, so I reached out. I would like to make songs with her too.

Westerman, that’s probably my most listened-to record. I think it came out in 2020. We had never met or talked, but I was a fan. I’m not very shy about it either, honestly. I’ve maintained some relationships with a couple of people where the beginning point was me being like, I’m completely obsessed with your music and everything, and make them send me songs. And then somehow I’ve held on to them.

I really loved his music. I’m really happy and love the remix he made too. It feels very much him. It’s like I got to visit wherever he goes when he makes things. I got to visit there, which is not something I thought about before I started making my own music. It’s a little layer to it now. I listen to music differently now than when I wasn’t making it. I can hear the making, or I wonder how, when people are singing or writing, how they did it, where they went to, or if they’re hippie about it at all, or if it’s very technical and clinical.

It has nothing to do with how organic the sounds are either. I’ve met, even more through this and other conversations I’ve had, electronic musicians who are way more woo-woo about their process and how they make things. They’re way more of a hippie about it than some of the acoustic-y-ass people I know who are just like, we’re going to write a song, and it’s this and this and this.

I’m very intuition-y. Then all the maths and all the real world stuff comes after, but some people start with the real world stuff. I’m always interested to hear how other people make things, and I’m always surprised at the answer. There are so many different ways to do it. Every time I go to make something, it’s with this kind of fear that I’m not going to be able to. I try to make an optimal situation for me, which all I have to go on is what I’ve done before. Then I end up making things I don’t like. I keep trying to add things in or push myself without getting too scared off or paralysed.

Listening to other people and how they work kind of gets rid of that mechanism in me. If somebody criticises me, I shut down in the middle of making something, which is how I usually am. I don’t like it at all, honestly. I’ll just put this on the radio: I don’t like to be scolded in any capacity. I really don’t care for it. I don’t take kindly to it. I’m very sensitive.

When I’m making music, this is my time to be like a baby and roll around and goo-goo-ga-ga stuff. I don’t like people being negative, but sometimes people have criticism and it can be a part of that. It can make the thing better, but it’s hard for me to hold that feeling in my body, because I just hear negative.

It’s this weird combination of feeling like a baby and being really vulnerable, but also having to really hype yourself up and kind of be bitchy and think people are going to want to hear what you have to say, or that what you’re doing is good enough to be recorded. You have to be vulnerable, but also strong and believing in yourself. It’s this really weird balance you have to find.

I write a lot about things I don’t really have built into me yet, but I want to. When the record came out and I wasn’t able to do some of the visual things I wanted to, or tour, or all these things I had planned, it was really hard for me to let go of it. I had this way I wanted everything to look and sound and feel.

This is a way for the songs to still be alive, doing things and going places. They don’t look or sound how I thought they were going to, but it’s still moving. That’s why you just have to wait most of the time. It’s a waiting thing. You never know where you’re going to be in a year, but you always feel like you do. I always feel so stuck, or like I know everything horrible that’s going to happen, but I don’t really. Honestly, sometimes I’m 100 per cent accurate. All the horrible stuff happens, but then it’s over or something else happens after that.

Simon: Then it’s never as bad as you think it would be, kind of thing.

Mike: Even though I’ve learned all that, it’s still so hard for me to let go, so hard for me to surrender. It’s really counterintuitive because a lot of times I feel like being in control is how I’m going to feel free or happy, when everything lines up the way I thought. When everything comes together the way I thought. But weirdly, embracing the chaos is the liberating thing. It’s really confusing sometimes.

Simon: With this remix collection, does it feel like an emotional gift in return for what you give in your music?

Mike: A really big gift, each one. It was really emotional for me, a lot because of the things we’re talking about. I haven’t felt very creative. I felt out of touch with every muscle, spiritual, physical. I felt like I was just laying down in every area of my being, in a funk, really. Then to get these remixes and hear all this vital energy and magic and stuff that feels far away. I felt included in it. It was like a little portal to some of mine, blown up or remembered.

Also a ticket to somebody else’s version of that, or somebody else who is still in touch with it, or even if it was just for this project, found it again. I don’t know everybody’s story, but they’re probably not as serious as I am about it.

Simon: Were there any interpretations that particularly surprised you when you first heard them?

Mike: I was familiar with everybody enough that even if my song was completely destroyed and rebuilt, I was expecting it from those specific people. I was expecting that energy. The only one was, Katie Dey did the very last song, ‘Borrowed Light’, and I’m very attached to that song. I was worried about a song that’s very emotional to me. I don’t know if it’s because it’s newer, but it makes me really emotional, that song.

All that stuff about not treating my songs as sacred, and blah, blah, blah. For that song, I felt it was a little sacred. But her remix is so beautiful and really satisfying. I guess that’s not the question, the question is if there was anything unexpected. I didn’t know if I was going to maintain a connection or have to fight to make a new one with that remix. But I didn’t. It was the same. Little portions of it magnified. It all felt satisfying.
